planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chansonette has a spreading, cascading habit well suited to hanging baskets, banks, and low walls.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Chansonette is a sasanqua camellia grown for its deep rose-pink, peony-form double flowers and its distinctive low, spreading, cascading growth habit, which sets it apart from the more upright sasanqua cultivars and makes it especially useful trained over a low wall, planted on a bank, or grown in a large hanging container. It blooms heavily in fall, offering reliable color when few other shrubs are flowering, and like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica cultivars. Prune only lightly to shape after flowering, since flower buds set later in the growing season.

common_name: White Doves Camellia (Compact Small-Flowered White Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; White Doves is a compact, spreading sasanqua camellia bearing small, anemone-form white flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. White Doves is a compact, spreading sasanqua camellia producing an abundance of small, pure white, anemone-form flowers with a fluffy center of golden stamens in a heavy fall flush, offering delicate, dove-like blooms when little else is in flower. Its manageable, spreading habit fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders without the size of many larger camellia cultivars. Like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica, blooming well in partial shade to full sun. Prune only lightly to shape after flowering, since flower buds set later in the growing season.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Jean May is a popular sasanqua camellia grown for its full, double, soft shell-pink flowers, considered among the more refined and exhibition-worthy blooms in the sasanqua group, produced in a heavy fall flush on an upright, moderately vigorous evergreen shrub. It offers reliable, showy color in the landscape during a season when few other shrubs are flowering, and like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica cultivars, blooming well from partial shade into full sun. common_name: Marge Miller Camellia (Spreading Groundcover-Type Pink Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Marge Miller has a low, wide, spreading habit that makes it useful as a large-scale groundcover or bank planting.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing plants to fill in as a spreading mass. Marge Miller is a sasanqua camellia grown for its low, wide, spreading, groundcover-like habit, quite different from the upright form of most camellias, producing semi-double pink flowers over the mounding foliage in a heavy fall flush. Its sprawling form makes it a distinctive choice for covering a bank, cascading over a low wall, or filling a large bed where a low-maintenance evergreen groundcover with fall bloom is wanted. Like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica, and needs only light shaping after flowering, since flower buds set later in the growing season.

common_name: Comanche Crape Myrtle (Coral-Pink Mildew-Resistant Indian-Series Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Comanche is a 1978 U.S. National Arboretum release from the Indian-series breeding program valued for coral-pink flowers and good mildew resistance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Comanche is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Indian-series crape myrtles, an interspecific hybrid of Lagerstroemia indica and Lagerstroemia fauriei released in 1978 for improved powdery mildew resistance over older all-indica cultivars, bearing large clusters of coral-pink flowers through summer on a medium-to-large tree. Like other Indian-series crape myrtles it develops attractive exfoliating bark and good fall foliage color, adding multi-season interest beyond the summer bloom. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Choctaw Crape Myrtle (Large-Flowered Bright Pink Indian-Series Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Choctaw is a tall U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series crape myrtle noted for very large flower clusters and among the best mildew resistance in the series.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun, allowing ample room for this tall, tree-form cultivar to reach its mature size. Choctaw is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Indian-series crape myrtles, prized for its clear bright pink flowers borne in exceptionally large clusters, among the largest of any crape myrtle cultivar, on a tall tree reaching up to 30 feet with age. It ranks among the most mildew-resistant cultivars in the Indian series, an important trait in the humid Gulf South, and develops attractive exfoliating bark for winter interest. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Osage Crape Myrtle (Semi-Dwarf Light Pink Cinnamon-Bark Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Osage, one of the earliest U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series releases (1975), is a semi-dwarf crape myrtle noted for smooth cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Osage was one of the earliest U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series crape myrtles, released in 1975, and remains valued for its light, clear pink flowers and especially smooth, glossy cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark, which many gardeners consider among the most attractive of any crape myrtle cultivar for winter interest. Its semi-dwarf, well-branched habit fits smaller landscapes better than some of the larger Indian-series introductions while still showing good resistance to powdery mildew. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Wichita Crape Myrtle (Large Lavender-Flowered Tree-Form Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Wichita is a large, tree-form U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series crape myrtle grown for bright lavender flower panicles and cinnamon-mahogany exfoliating bark.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving this large tree-form cultivar plenty of room to mature. Wichita is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Indian-series crape myrtles, producing bright lavender flower panicles through summer on a large, upright tree, with richly colored cinnamon-to-mahogany exfoliating bark that provides striking winter interest once the leaves drop. Its size and vigor make it well suited as a specimen shade tree or street tree in larger landscapes rather than a foundation shrub. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Arapaho Crape Myrtle (True Red Upright Crape Myrtle with Dark Fall Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Arapaho is a later U.S. National Arboretum release bred for improved true-red flower color and mildew resistance on a tall, upright tree.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Arapaho is a later U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series release bred to improve on earlier red-flowered crape myrtles, combining true, vivid red summer flowers with strong resistance to powdery mildew and dark maroon-red fall foliage color that extends the tree's seasonal interest well past bloom time. The tall, upright habit suits it to specimen or street tree use in larger Gulf South landscapes. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Fantasy Crape Myrtle (Tall White-Flowered Fauriei Selection with Cinnamon Bark)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fantasy is a pure Lagerstroemia fauriei selection, rather than an indica hybrid, grown mainly for its outstanding cinnamon exfoliating bark and very large mature size.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun, siting this large, tree-form selection where it has ample room to grow into a substantial shade tree. Fantasy is a selection of Lagerstroemia fauriei, the Japanese species behind the mildew resistance and exfoliating bark of the modern Indian-series hybrids, grown less for its relatively modest white flower clusters than for its own outstanding qualities: smooth, richly colored cinnamon bark that peels in large sheets, and a fast-growing habit that can reach 30 to 40 feet, among the tallest of any crape myrtle. It is essentially free of powdery mildew, a trait inherited from its Lagerstroemia fauriei parentage. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural form; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter as the tree matures into a fine specimen or shade tree.
